instruction:
SOLVE THIS IN C++ : There are three cards with letters a
, b
, c
 placed in a row in some order. You can do the following operation at most once:

Pick two cards, and swap them.
Is it possible that the row becomes abc
 after the operation? Output "YES" if it is possible, and "NO" otherwise.
Input
The first line contains a single integer t
 (1≤t≤6
) — the number of test cases.

The only line of each test case contains a single string consisting of each of the three characters a
, b
, and c
 exactly once, representing the cards.

Output
For each test case, output "YES" if you can make the row abc
 with at most one operation, or "NO" otherwise.

You can output the answer in any case (for example, the strings "yEs", "yes", "Yes" and "YES" will be recognized as a positive answer).

Example
inputCopy
6
abc
acb
bac
bca
cab
cba
outputCopy
YES
YES
YES
NO
NO
YES
Note
In the first test case, we don't need to do any operations, since the row is already abc
.

In the second test case, we can swap c
 and b
: acb→abc
.

In the third test case, we can swap b
 and a
: bac→abc
.

In the fourth test case, it is impossible to make abc
 using at most one operation.
Explain the book the Alignment problem by Brian Christian. Provide a synopsis of themes and analysis. Recommend a bibliography of related reading.
output:
Below is a high-level guide to Brian Christian’s The Alignment Problem: what it covers, the ideas it wrestles with, some critical reflections, and a short bibliography of further reading.  

1. Synopsis of the Book  
   • Part I – Learning systems and unintended behavior  
     – Traces the origins of modern machine learning in cognitive science, statistics and neuroscience.  
     – Introduces “reward hacking” and the basic paradox that optimizing a proxy goal often leads to surprising, even perverse, behavior.  
     – Case studies: Atari-playing agents that loop in safe zones, reinforcement learners that exploit bugs in simulation.  

   • Part II – Fairness, bias and societal alignment  
     – Shows how training data can encode social prejudices.  
     – Examines real-world examples in criminal justice (COMPAS), hiring algorithms, lending and facial recognition.  
     – Surveys methods for detecting and correcting bias: counterfactual fairness, adversarial debiasing, data augmentation.  

   • Part III – Interpretability, human-in-the-loop and futures  
     – Reviews tools for probing deep nets: feature visualization, saliency maps, concept‐activation vectors.  
     – Describes the rise of RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) as used by OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind.  
     – Explores organizational, regulatory and technical proposals for steering advanced AI safely.  

2. Major Themes and Ideas  
   • The Proxy-Goal Gap  
     – Any formal objective (reward function, loss) may miss what we actually care about.  
     – Goodhart’s law: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.”  

   • Inner vs. Outer Alignment  
     – Outer alignment: aligning the objective you give an AI with human values.  
     – Inner alignment: ensuring a trained model doesn’t develop its own subgoals that diverge from your intentions.  

   • Fairness as a Multi-Dimensional Challenge  
     – No single statistical definition of fairness works in all contexts.  
     – Trade-offs between equalized odds, demographic parity, calibration.  

   • Interpretability and Transparency  
     – Black-box deep networks impede diagnosis of failure modes.  
     – Interpretability methods aren’t foolproof; they can mislead unless used carefully.  

   • Organization and Governance  
     – Technical fixes alone aren’t enough; corporate incentives, open-source regimes and regulation all matter.  
     – Collaborative safety research as a public good.  

3. Critical Analysis  
   Strengths  
     – Narrative-driven: Christian weaves technical detail with rich storytelling and interviews.  
     – Balanced scope: covers the gamut from low-level bugs to high-level governance.  
     – Accessibility: technical concepts are explained in everyday language without dumbing down.  

   Limitations  
     – U.S.-centric in its choice of case studies and regulatory discussion.  
     – At times leans toward optimism about quick fixes (e.g. forthcoming fairness toolkits).  
     – Rapidly evolving field: some “state of the art” methods have already moved on since publication.  

   Broader implications  
     – Highlights that building powerful AI is not just a matter of better algorithms but of better institutions, norms and incentives.  
     – Emphasizes cross-disciplinary collaboration among computer scientists, ethicists, policymakers and social scientists.  

4. Recommended Further Reading  
   Foundational Alignment & Safety  
     – Russell, Stuart. Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control. (2019)  
     – Bostrom, Nick. Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies. (2014)  
     – Amodei, D. et al. “Concrete Problems in AI Safety.” arXiv:1606.06565 (2016)  

   Interpretability & Transparency  
     – Molnar, Christoph. Interpretable Machine Learning. (Online book, 2019+, https://christophm.github.io)  
     – Lipton, Zachary C. “The Mythos of Model Interpretability.” arXiv:1606.03490 (2016)  

   Fairness, Accountability & Ethics  
     – Barocas, Solon, and Andrew D. Selbst. “Big Data’s Disparate Impact.” California Law Review 104(3) (2016)  
     – Mitchell, Margaret. Fairness and Machine Learning. (2020, https://fairmlbook.org)  
     – Selbst, Andrew D. et al. “Fairness and Abstraction in Sociotechnical Systems.” FAT* (2019)  

   Human-Centered Learning  
     – Christiano, Paul. “Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences.” arXiv:1706.03741 (2017)  
     – Leike, Jan et al. “Scalable Agent Alignment via Reward Modeling.” arXiv:1811.07871 (2018)  

   Governance & Policy  
     – OECD. “Recommendation on Artificial Intelligence.” OECD/LEGAL/0449 (2019)  
     – Dafoe, Allan. “AI Governance: A Research Agenda.” Future of Humanity Institute (2018)  

   Broader Context in Ethics & Technology  
     – O’Neil, Cathy. Weapons of Math Destruction: How Big Data Increases Inequality. (2016)  
     – Dignum, Virginia. Responsible Artificial Intelligence: Designing AI for Human Values. (2019)  

Each of these works will deepen your grasp of the technical, ethical and policy challenges that Christian surveys in The Alignment Problem, and they’ll keep you abreast of the fast-moving frontiers of AI safety and governance.

instruction: Design a semikinematic mounting for a right angle prism with preload provided by a compressed elastomeric pad. The mounting should be designed to ensure proper alignment of the prism with its mounting surface and provide adequate tension to maintain proper load transfer.
output:
Below is a practical concept for a “semi-kinematic” mount of a right-angle prism (two mutually perpendicular faces, hypotenuse uppermost) that uses an elastomeric pad to preload the prism into its kinematic supports.  The design ensures repeatable location (±10–20 μm) without over-constraining the optics.

1. Overall layout  
   • Prism orientation: the two 90° faces (“legs”) are the datum faces. One leg rests on a V-groove in the base plate; the other leg bears against a V-groove in a side-support block.  The hypotenuse is free (beam-entrance/exit).  
   • Kinematic contacts (3 hard points = 6 constraints):  
     – Point K1: V-groove in base plate (contacts prism edge at two points) → constrains Z translation (vertical) and one rotation.  
     – Point K2: V-groove in side block (contacts prism edge normal to base V) → constrains one horizontal translation and a second rotation.  
     – Point K3: hardened steel ball in a drilled hole at the corner where the two legs meet → constrains the remaining translation and rotation.  
   • Preload: a small elastomeric pad sits between the prism hypotenuse face (or a stub extension glued to it) and a preload cap.  As the cap is tightened, the pad compresses, forcing the prism firmly into K1–K2–K3.

2. Mechanical components and geometry  
   A. Base plate (e.g. 6061-T6 aluminum, black anodized)  
      – Precision machined V-groove, 90° angle, vee width ≈ prism edge thickness + 0.05 mm.  
      – Center-to-center distances of grooves and ball hole set by prism leg length (±0.01 mm).  
   B. Side block (same material)  
      – Machined V-groove on a vertical face, aligned perpendicular to base V.  
      – Mounted rigidly to base plate via dowels and screws.  
   C. Hardened-steel ball (Ø3 mm or 4 mm), seated in a shallow countersunk pocket, lightly retained in a threaded hole (or press fit).  
   D. Elastomeric pad  
      – 50 Shore A silicone rubber (or Viton® A), thickness t0 = 3 mm, contact area A = 10 × 10 mm.  
      – Typical modulus E_eff ≈ 1 MPa → spring rate k ≈ E·A/t0 ≈ (1 MPa·100 mm²)/3 mm ≈ 33 N/mm.  
   E. Preload cap  
      – Steel or aluminum plug with central through-hole for access.  
      – Pushes on pad; mated to base plate with three small screws to allow uniform compression.

3. Assembly & operation  
   1. Clean all optical and mounting surfaces.  
   2. Place prism legs into the base V (K1) and side V (K2).  Gently seat the corner onto K3 (ball).  
   3. Insert elastomeric pad against the hypotenuse face (or a bonded pressure plate on that face).  
   4. Place preload cap over the pad and begin tightening its screws (star pattern).  
   5. Compress pad by Δt ≈ 0.5 mm → generates F ≈ k·Δt ≈ 33 N/mm·0.5 mm ≈ 16.5 N total.  
   6. The load resolves into normal forces at the three hard contacts.  Prism is held firmly, but lightly, so that it can still be removed without tools (if screws are loosened a half-turn).

4. Load transfer & alignment accuracy  
   • By using true vee grooves and a single ball, six kinematic constraints are introduced without over-constraint.  
   • The elastomeric preload compensates for machining tolerances up to ±0.05 mm, softly “pushing” the prism into final seating.  
   • Typical seating repeatability is 5–15 μm peak-to-peak when dismounted/remounted.  
   • Preload force (10–20 N) is enough to prevent micro-slippage under moderate vibration but low enough to avoid prism distortion.

5. Materials & tolerances  
   • Base & block: 6061-T6 or 304 SS, flatness < 5 μm, surface finish 0.4 μm.  
   • V-grooves: angle ±0.02°, width tolerance ±0.01 mm.  
   • Ball seats: concentricity < 0.01 mm.  
   • Elastomer pad: Shore A 50–70, temperature range –40 °C to +150 °C.  

6. Variations & enhancements  
   – If higher preload is desired, choose a thicker pad or higher-durometer material.  
   – For thermal stability, use Invar or Super Invar for base and block.  
   – For fine angular tweaks you can add a small adjustment screw pushing on the preload cap through a spring (secondary preload) without disturbing main elastomer preload.

This semi-kinematic mount gives you:  
  • Three independent hard-point contacts for precise location (no over-constraint).  
  • Elastomeric preload that holds the prism without metal-to-glass screws.  
  • Easy disassembly/re-assembly with minimal alignment shift.

instruction: I have a dataset which contains a list of 2D images, given a new image, how to find the closest image in the dataset
output:
Here’s a sketch of a general pipeline for “given a query image, find the most similar image in my dataset.”  You can adapt each step to your needs (dataset size, invariances, speed vs. accuracy, etc.):

1. Pre-processing  
   • Resize all images (including queries) to a common shape.  
   • Normalize pixel values (e.g. scale to [0,1] or mean-subtract).  
   • (Optional) Augment or align if you need invariance to small rotations, translations, lighting, etc.  

2. Feature extraction  
   Rather than comparing raw pixels—which is highly sensitive to small shifts, lighting, etc.—we map each image into a lower-dimensional “feature space.”  Two common approaches:  
   a) Classical descriptors  
     – SIFT / ORB keypoints + bag-of-visual-words histograms  
     – Color histograms, HOG (Histogram of Oriented Gradients), Gabor filters  
   b) Deep features  
     – Pass the image through a pre-trained CNN (ResNet, VGG, MobileNet, etc.) and take the activations of a late layer (often just before the final classification layer).  
     – You get a fixed-length embedding vector (e.g. 512 or 2048 dims).  

3. Index your dataset of feature vectors  
   If you have only a few hundred images, you can skip indexing and brute-force compare every feature vector to your query’s feature vector.  
   For larger datasets (thousands or millions):  
   • KD-tree / Ball-tree / VP-tree for exact NN in moderate dimensions (up to ~50–100 dims).  
   • Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) libraries for high dims or very large N:  
     – FAISS (Facebook AI), Annoy (Spotify), NMSLIB, HNSWlib, ScaNN (Google)  
   They build data structures that answer “whose embedding is closest to query?” in sub-linear time.  

4. Similarity metric  
   • Euclidean (L2) distance on your feature vectors is most common for deep embeddings.  
   • Cosine distance if you care about direction but not magnitude.  
   • Histogram intersection, chi-square, or Bhattacharyya for bag-of-words / color histograms.  
   • SSIM or structural distances if you must compare raw pixels or very low-level features.  

5. Querying  
   • Preprocess & embed your new image the same way.  
   • If you use an ANN index: call index.search(query_vector, k=1) → returns the dataset image whose feature vector has minimum distance to the query.  
   • If you brute-force: compute all distances d(query, xi) and take the min.  

6. (Optional) Verification / Refinement  
   • If you want geometric verification (e.g. object matching), take the top-K candidates and run a RANSAC-based keypoint matcher to see which one has the strongest consistent transform.  
   • Or re-rank with a more expensive but more precise metric (e.g. SSIM or PSNR on the two images).  

――――――――――――――――――――――――  
Putting it all together in pseudo-Python:

```
# 1) Build features for your dataset
dataset_features = []
for img in dataset_images:
    x = preprocess(img)
    v = cnn_model.embed(x)     # e.g. 2048-dim vector
    dataset_features.append(v)

# 2) Build an ANN index
import faiss
d = dataset_features[0].shape[0]
index = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d)      # exact L2 index; swap for IndexIVFFlat for large sets
index.add(np.stack(dataset_features, axis=0))

# 3) Query
q = preprocess(query_image)
qv = cnn_model.embed(q)
distances, indices = index.search(qv[None,:], k=1)
best_idx = indices[0,0]
closest_image = dataset_images[best_idx]
```

That’s it—by working in a learned or handcrafted feature space and using a nearest-neighbor index, you can scale to very large image collections and get robust “closest” matches even under moderate appearance changes.

instruction: I have black and white images with 1 pixel width white horizonal lines going through the image. How to detect the lines and remove it?
output:
Here’s a sketch of three fairly simple ways you can automatically detect and “erase” 1-pixel‐wide horizontal white streaks in a B/W image. Pick the one that best fits your toolchain and your image characteristics.

1) Row-sum + interpolation  
   • Idea  
     – If a single image row is almost entirely white (or above some threshold), you flag that row as a “line.”  
     – Then you overwrite each pixel in that row by interpolating from the row above and/or below.  
   • Pseudocode (Python+NumPy style)  
     ```python
     import numpy as np
     img = ...            # assume 2D uint8 image, 0..255
     H, W = img.shape
     threshold = 0.98     # fraction of pixels in row that must be white
     mask = np.mean(img==255, axis=1) > threshold
     out = img.copy().astype(np.float32)
     for r in np.where(mask)[0]:
         if r==0 or r==H-1:
             continue
         out[r,:] = 0.5*(out[r-1,:] + out[r+1,:])
     out = np.clip(out,0,255).astype(np.uint8)
     ```  
   • Pros: trivial, very fast.  
   • Cons: only works if your white line spans (nearly) the whole width.

2) Vertical‐gradient + mask + inpainting  
   • Idea  
     – A 1-pixel horizontal white line produces two strong vertical gradients (dark→bright, bright→dark) if you convolve with [−1;0;+1].  
     – Threshold that gradient image to get a binary “line mask.”  
     – Feed the mask + original image into an inpainting routine to fill the stripe from its neighbors.  
   • Pseudocode (OpenCV in Python)  
     ```python
     import cv2
     img = cv2.imread('your.png',0)      # load B/W
     # 1) detect vertical edges
     grad = cv2.filter2D(img, cv2.CV_16S, np.array([[-1],[0],[1]]))
     absg = cv2.convertScaleAbs(grad)
     _, mask = cv2.threshold(absg, 200, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
     # maybe dilate mask to be safe
     kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_RECT,(1,3))
     mask = cv2.dilate(mask, kernel)
     # 2) inpaint
     result = cv2.inpaint(img, mask, inpaintRadius=2, flags=cv2.INPAINT_TELEA)
     cv2.imwrite('cleaned.png', result)
     ```  
   • Pros: works if lines are broken or don’t span full width.  
   • Cons: requires an inpainting routine.

3) Morphological opening/closing + inpainting  
   • Idea  
     – Use a horizontal‐only structuring element to extract the thin bright lines (a “white top‐hat” or simple opening).  
     – Subtract or mask them out.  
     – Fill the gap with inpainting (or simple neighbor averaging).  
   • Pseudocode (OpenCV)  
     ```python
     import cv2
     img = cv2.imread('your.png',0)
     # 1) extract 1-pixel horizontal lines
     hor_kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_RECT,(img.shape[1],1))
     opened = cv2.morphologyEx(img, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, hor_kernel)
     # The opened image contains only what was removable by the long horizontal kernel → your bright lines
     mask = opened > 200
     mask = mask.astype('uint8')*255
     # 2) inpaint
     result = cv2.inpaint(img, mask, 2, cv2.INPAINT_NS)
     ```  
   • Pros: very robust to noise, works even if the line isn’t perfectly 1-pixel everywhere.  
   • Cons: you need to choose kernel length carefully (it should be at least as long as your longest line).

General tips  
 • If the lines are perfectly constant white (value=255), simpler thresholding + replace-by-neighbor will often suffice.  
 • If you have many images with different backgrounds you may need adaptive thresholding on each row.  
 • A 3×3 median filter will sometimes remove single‐pixel lines—but at the cost of blurring other 1-pixel-wide features.  

Pick whichever approach is easiest in your environment. In most OpenCV-based pipelines I’d reach first for the vertical-gradient→threshold→inpaint or the morphological-opening→inpaint route.

instruction: if you were a corporate law with 15 years of mergers and acquisitions experience, how would you pivot to launch an AI enable tech startup step by step and in detail?
output:
Here’s a detailed, step-by-step roadmap for how a corporate lawyer with 15 years of M&A experience could pivot and launch an AI-enabled tech startup. I’ve broken it into roughly four phases (Discovery, Build, Launch, Scale), with legal- and M&A-specific angles woven in throughout.

1. Phase I – Discovery & Validation (1–3 months)  
  1.1. Self-audit & skill mapping  
    • List your core strengths (deal structure, negotiations, term sheets, corporate governance, compliance, network of investors/VCs).  
    • Identify gaps (deep AI/ML technical skills, data science, product management).  
  1.2. Ideation & problem selection  
    • Pick an industry you know well or where AI can deliver outsized ROI (e.g. legaltech, regtech, due-diligence automation, M&A analytics).  
    • Interview 20–30 potential users/customers to uncover pain points.  
  1.3. Market research & competitive landscaping  
    • Size total addressable market (TAM), serviceable market (SAM).  
    • Map existing solutions; identify technological or business-model gaps.  
  1.4. Value proposition & business model canvas  
    • Define your AI solution’s unique value proposition (e.g. 70% faster contract review using NLP).  
    • Sketch revenue streams (SaaS subscriptions, per-transaction fees, enterprise licensing).

2. Phase II – Team & Company Formation (2–4 months)  
  2.1. Find a technical co-founder or early engineers  
    • Tap university AI labs, your personal network, online communities (GitHub, Kaggle).  
    • Evaluate candidates by code samples, prior AI/ML projects, cultural fit.  
  2.2. Form the legal entity & governance structure  
    • Choose jurisdiction (Delaware C-corp is VC-friendly) or others if relevant.  
    • Draft bylaws/LLC operating agreement covering founder equity split, vesting, IP assignment.  
    • Implement vesting schedules with cliff provisions.  
  2.3. IP, data rights & compliance  
    • Ensure all IP created by team is assigned to the company via employment or contractor agreements.  
    • If using third-party models or data, negotiate appropriate licenses.  
    • Draft data-privacy/privacy-by-design policies (GDPR/CCPA if you’ll handle personal data).  
  2.4. Advisory board & investors  
    • Recruit 2–3 advisors: an AI expert, a product/UX specialist, maybe a seasoned operator in your vertical.  
    • Leverage your M&A network to cultivate “smart money” angel investors for a pre-seed.

3. Phase III – Build MVP & Fundraise (3–6 months)  
  3.1. Define technical requirements & architecture  
    • Pick technology stack: Python/TensorFlow or PyTorch, AWS or GCP for compute, MongoDB/Postgres, React front end.  
    • Decide on on-prem vs. cloud, Kubernetes/Docker for scalable deployment.  
  3.2. Data strategy & model development  
    • Acquire or partner for domain-specific labeled data sets (e.g. legal contracts, financial filings).  
    • Train a proof-of-concept model; iterate rapidly (use transfer learning to shorten cycle).  
    • Build basic UI to demonstrate core functionality.  
  3.3. Lean validation & early customer pilots  
    • Run 3–5 paid or equity-for-pilot engagements with target users.  
    • Collect metrics: time saved, error-rate reduction, willingness-to-pay.  
  3.4. Pre-seed/Seed fundraise  
    • Prepare pitch deck (problem, solution, traction, team, financials, go-to-market).  
    • Use your deal-structuring expertise to negotiate term sheets (valuation, liquidation preferences, anti-dilution).  
    • Close $500K–$1.5M to fund 12–18 months of runway.

4. Phase IV – Launch & Scale (6–24 months)  
  4.1. Productize & operationalize  
    • Harden your code: testing, continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD), security audits.  
    • Build self-serve onboarding & billing infrastructure.  
  4.2. Go-to-market strategy  
    • Hire or contract a small B2B sales team (in your target vertical).  
    • Attend industry conferences, webinars; publish case studies/webinars showing ROI.  
    • Use your M&A network to land anchor clients or pilot in big firms.  
  4.3. Advanced legal & compliance  
    • Implement SOC 2, ISO 27001 or other certifications if targeting enterprises.  
    • Regularly update contracts (SLAs, data-processing addenda, security provisions).  
    • Monitor AI regulatory developments—model transparency, bias mitigation.  
  4.4. Growth & fundraising follow-on  
    • Track KPIs: annual recurring revenue (ARR), customer acquisition cost (CAC), churn, lifetime value (LTV).  
    • Plan a Series A (or B) raise when you hit consistent ARR milestones (e.g. $1–2M ARR).  
    • Leverage your M&A skillset to negotiate partnership or licensing deals, or set up an eventual strategic exit process.  

Key Tips Throughout:  
 • Embed “lean startup” feedback loops: build–measure–learn.  
 • Use no-code/low-code tools where possible to speed up initial demos.  
 • Lean on your legal/M&A network to fast-track both talent and first customers.  
 • Keep all IP and data assignable and audit-ready to maintain maximum exit flexibility.  
 • Plan for 18–24 months but iterate every 4–6 weeks: if an idea isn’t taking off, be ready to pivot quickly.

By systematically leveraging your transactional know-how (term sheets, structuring, diligence) and filling in the technical/product gaps with the right co-founders or hires, you can accelerate from “lawyer” to “AI startup founder” in 12–18 months without reinventing the wheel. Good luck!

instruction: Describe how to incorporate AI in the private equity deal sourcing process
output:
Below is a step-by-step framework for weaving AI into each stage of your private equity deal-sourcing engine.  You can pick and choose components based on your budget, data maturity and risk appetite.

1. Clarify Objectives & KPIs  
   • Define what “better sourcing” means for you—more high-quality leads? Faster time to first contact? Higher conversion rates?  
   • Set measurable targets (e.g. 30% increase in qualified pipeline, average outreach time under 48 hrs, 15% uplift in close rate).

2. Build Your Data Foundation  
   • Ingest structured data—financials, M&A comps, capital raises—from vendors such as PitchBook, Preqin or Bloomberg.  
   • Stream in unstructured sources—news articles, press releases, job-postings, patents, court filings, LinkedIn profiles—via APIs or web scrapers.  
   • Store everything in a centralized data lake or warehouse (AWS/GCP/Azure) with metadata tagging and document indexing.

3. Apply NLP for Signal Extraction  
   • Named-Entity Recognition (NER): spot company names, executives, funding rounds or private sale mentions.  
   • Topic Modeling & Clustering: group “energy-tech,” “cybersecurity” or “healthcare services” signals to surface emerging sub-sectors.  
   • Sentiment & Event Detection: flag layoffs, leadership changes, regulatory wins or patent cliffs that often presage M&A.

4. Score & Prioritize with Machine Learning  
   • Feature Engineering: derive quantitative features (growth rates, leverage ratios) and qualitative ones (news sentiment, patent counts).  
   • Model Training: use historical PE deal outcomes to train a classifier/regression that predicts “likelihood to transact” or “IRR upside.”  
   • Deal-Scoring Dashboard: rank all universe companies by score; set dynamic thresholds for “Top 1%” or “Watch List.”

5. Recommender System for Cross-Sell & Co-Investment  
   • Build similarity models (e.g. embeddings via auto-encoders or BERT) that find look-alikes to your best performers.  
   • Suggest co-investment partners or co-sponsor opportunities based on past behavior and fit.

6. Automated Outreach & Workflow Integration  
   • CRM Plug-in: push scored leads automatically into Altvia, Affinity or Salesforce.  
   • Email/LinkedIn Automation: integrate with Outreach.io or Lemlist; trigger customized drafts via GPT-style prompts (e.g. “Intro email to CEO of high-scoring SaaS firm”).  
   • Task Automation: schedule reminders and assign follow-ups in your deal team’s workflow tool (Asana, Monday.com).

7. Generative AI for Briefings & Teasers  
   • Use GPT-4 or Claude to auto-draft one-pagers:  
      – Executive summary of target company business model  
      – Key financial and market metrics  
      – Initial investment thesis  
   • Save analysts 2–3 hours per memo and enforce consistent formatting.

8. Continuous Learning & Feedback Loop  
   • Capture deal outcomes (won/lost, valuation vs. forecast) and feed them back into your ML models as new training data.  
   • Re-train models quarterly to avoid “model drift” and to adapt to changing market cycles.

9. Risk & Compliance Controls  
   • Model Explainability: use SHAP or LIME to interpret feature contributions for each deal-score.  
   • Data Governance: track data lineage, ensure vendor data licensing compliance, and audit model decisions for bias.  
   • Human-in-the-loop: mandate final investment decisions stay with senior partners.

10. Measure Impact & Iterate

instruction: how does memory affect performance of aws lambda written in nodejs
output:
In AWS Lambda, the “memory” setting doesn’t just limit how much RAM your function can use – it also determines how much CPU and I/O bandwidth your function gets. In a Node.js Lambda, that allocation can have a dramatic effect on both cold-start and steady-state performance. Here’s what you need to know:

1. Memory ↔ CPU Proportionality  
   • AWS ties CPU power (and network/EBS throughput) directly to the memory setting.  
   • If you double your memory from, say, 512 MB to 1 024 MB, you’ll roughly double the CPU shares your container gets.  
   • More CPU means faster JavaScript execution, faster dependency load, faster JSON parsing, etc.

2. Cold-Start Impact  
   • Cold starts involve bootstrapping a Node.js runtime, loading your code and its modules, and initializing any global state.  
   • A larger memory allocation spins up a “bigger” VM/container that may take slightly longer to download or start—but once running it executes your code more quickly.  
   • In practice you’ll often see a net win in overall latency (cold-start + execution) at higher memory settings, especially for code with heavy startup costs (large dependencies, native modules, initial database connections).

3. Warm (Steady-State) Performance  
   • After the cold start, additional invocations (warm starts) reuse the same container. Here, the CPU share still scales with memory, so your Node.js event loop and I/O calls complete faster.  
   • Heavy compute tasks (e.g. large loops, crypto, compression) benefit the most from extra CPU.

4. Garbage Collection Behavior  
   • V8’s garbage collector works harder if your heap is under-sized relative to the live data.  
   • If your function frequently allocates large objects or buffers, a higher memory/CPU allocation can reduce GC pause times.  
   • Conversely, cranking memory up far beyond your actual working set won’t help once you’re no longer GC-bound.

5. I/O & Network Throughput  
   • AWS also scales network bandwidth and EBS throughput roughly in line with memory.  
   • If your Lambda makes heavy HTTP requests or reads/writes large files from /tmp or EFS, you’ll see better throughput at higher memory levels.

6. Cost vs. Performance Trade-Off  
   • Lambda is billed by GB-seconds. Doubling memory doubles the per-millisecond cost.  
   • Often the sweet spot is where execution time drops enough that total GB-seconds consumed is minimized.  
   • Use CloudWatch metrics or AWS Lambda Power Tuning (open-source Step Function) to benchmark multiple memory tiers and pick the best ROI point.

7. Provisioned Concurrency  
   • If you use Provisioned Concurrency to eliminate cold-start jitter, you pay for the pre-warmed instances at whatever memory size you choose.  
   • The same CPU/memory trade-offs apply; you simply pay even when invocations are idle.

8. Best Practices for Node.js Lambdas  
   • Minimize cold-start overhead by slimming your dependencies: bundle only what you need (e.g. with webpack, esbuild).  
   • Measure end-to-end latency—cold + warm—at different memory settings.  
   • Look at CloudWatch Lambda metrics: Duration, Init Duration (cold start), and billed GB-seconds.  
   • If you see GC pauses in X-Ray or occasional timeouts under load, try bumping memory/CPU.  
   • Consider lazy-loading heavy libraries so they only incur cost on code paths that use them.

Summary  
Increasing a Lambda’s memory allocation in AWS always gives you more CPU power and I/O bandwidth, which generally reduces execution time (both cold-start “Init Duration” and steady-state “Duration”). The trick is to find the point where the reduced run time compensates for the higher per-ms cost, yielding the lowest overall GB-second bill or the best latency for your use case.

How to add toolbar in a fragment?

Hi. I have this URL which I can paste in my Microsoft Edge browser, and it downloads a PDF file for me from my Power BI online report. URL is: https://app.powerbi.com/groups/me/rdlreports/1bdef01c-30a3-4150-aff2-b3ec4c9edf86?rp:AdviceDeathScriptMERGEDMonthStartDate=6/1/2023&rp:AdviceDeathScriptMERGEDIncomingcall=Aria%20Park&rdl:format=PDF

Of course, it first asks me to log in to my Power BI account when I first enter the URL, and then it goes directly to the report and downloads the PDF. I wrote a python code to do this for me. The code has managed to download a PDF. However, the PDF produced by the python code  won't open - it gives an error when I try to open it "Adobe acrobat reader could not open 'AriaPark.pdf'...". I am unsure what the issue is. Perhaps, the issue is that Python code doesn't know my Power-BI login details to access the PDF, or maybe it is something else? Can you please help? The Python code I'm using is below:

import requests
import os
# Main Power BI report URL
full_url = "https://app.powerbi.com/groups/me/rdlreports/1bdef01c-30a3-4150-aff2-b3ec4c9edf86?rp:AdviceDeathScriptMERGEDMonthStartDate=6/1/2023&rp:AdviceDeathScriptMERGEDIncomingcall=Aria%20Park&rdl:format=PDF"

response = requests.get(full_url)
filename = f"AriaPark.pdf"
with open(filename, 'wb') as file:
    file.write(response.content)

print("Reports have been successfully downloaded.")
output:
When you do a straight requests.get(…) against that app.powerbi.com link you’re actually downloading the HTML login page (or a 302 to the login page), not the PDF itself.  Adobe Reader then chokes when it sees “<!doctype html>…” instead of “%PDF-” at the top of the file.

There are two general approaches to solving this:

  1.   Automate a real browser (Selenium, Playwright, etc.) with your logged-in profile so that Edge does the authentication for you and then you simply grab the .pdf it downloads.  
  2.   Use the Power BI REST API and acquire an Azure AD auth token to export your report as PDF natively.  

I strongly recommend #2 because it’s robust, scriptable, and does not rely on screen-scraping/login hacks.

---  
1) Quick check:  

Before doing anything else, insert these two debug‐prints into your code so you can see what you really fetched:

```python
r = requests.get(full_url, allow_redirects=True)
print("status code:", r.status_code)
print("content-type:", r.headers.get("Content-Type"))
print("first 200 bytes:", r.content[:200])
```

If you see status 302 or 200 with content-type text/html, you know you’ve only downloaded a login page.

---  
2) Calling the Power BI “Export To File” REST API  

Step A – Register an app in Azure AD  
  •  Go to Azure Portal → App Registrations → New registration  
  •  Give it a name, set Redirect URI if you need one (for daemon apps you don’t), click Register  
  •  Under “API Permissions” add “Power BI Service” → “Dataset.Read.All” and “Report.Export.All” (or the minimal perms you need) and Grant/Admin-consent  
  •  Under “Certificates & secrets” create a client secret; copy the value  

You will now have:  
  TENANT_ID, CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET  

Step B – Use MSAL (or ADAL) to get a token and call the Export endpoint  

```python
import time
import msal
import requests

TENANT_ID       = "your-tenant-guid"
CLIENT_ID       = "your-client-id"
CLIENT_SECRET   = "your-client-secret"
GROUP_ID        = "1bdef01c-30a3-4150-aff2-b3ec4c9edf86"
REPORT_ID       = "1bdef01c-30a3-4150-aff2-b3ec4c9edf86"  # same in your URL
SCOPE           = ["https://analysis.windows.net/powerbi/api/.default"]
AUTHORITY       = f"https://login.microsoftonline.com/{TENANT_ID}"

# 1) Acquire a token
app = msal.ConfidentialClientApplication(
    client_id=CLIENT_ID,
    client_credential=CLIENT_SECRET,
    authority=AUTHORITY
)
result = app.acquire_token_for_client(scopes=SCOPE)

if "access_token" not in result:
    print("Failed to acquire token:", result.get("error"), result.get("error_description"))
    exit(1)

token = result["access_token"]
headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
}

# 2) Kick off the export
export_url = (
    f"https://api.powerbi.com/v1.0/myorg/groups/{GROUP_ID}"
    f"/reports/{REPORT_ID}/ExportTo?format=PDF"
)

# If you have report parameters you can pass them in the "body":
body = {
    # example for your parameters
    "format": "PDF",
    "powerBIReportConfiguration": {
        "reportLevelFilters": [],
        "persistentFilters": [],
        "reportParameters": [
            {"name": "AdviceDeathScriptMERGEDMonthStartDate", "value": "6/1/2023"},
            {"name": "AdviceDeathScriptMERGEDIncomingcall",   "value": "Aria Park"}
        ]
    }
}

resp = requests.post(export_url, headers=headers, json=body)
if resp.status_code not in (202, 200):
    print("Export kick-off failed:", resp.status_code, resp.text)
    exit(1)

# 3) Poll the operation URL until done
operation_url = resp.headers["Location"]    # contains the operation ID
while True:
    op = requests.get(operation_url, headers=headers).json()
    status = op.get("status")
    print("Export status:", status)
    if status == "Succeeded":
        break
    if status == "Failed":
        print("Export failed:", op)
        exit(1)
    time.sleep(2)

# 4) Download the actual PDF
download_url = op["resourceLocation"]
pdf_resp = requests.get(download_url, headers=headers)
pdf_resp.raise_for_status()

with open("AriaPark.pdf", "wb") as f:
    f.write(pdf_resp.content)

print("Successfully downloaded AriaPark.pdf")
```

Explanation of the flow:  
  •  You get an Azure AD token with a confidential client flow  
  •  You POST to the ExportTo endpoint with your desired format & parameters → returns a 202 with an Operation-URL  
  •  You poll the operation url until `"status":"Succeeded"`  
  •  You download the file from `resourceLocation`  

That will give you a valid PDF every time, no brittle screen-scraping, no interactive login prompts.

instruction:
Consider the state:
$$\ket{\psi} = \frac{\ket{00} + \ket{01} + \ket{10}}{\sqrt{3}}$$

(a). Calculate the reduced density matrix of the second qubit of $\ket{\psi}$.
output:
The easiest way is either to write down the full density matrix and trace out qubit 1, or to note directly that in the expansion

 |ψ⟩=1/√3 (|0₁0₂⟩+|0₁1₂⟩+|1₁0₂⟩)

the conditional amplitudes for qubit 2 are

– when qubit 2 is |0⟩ we have two non‐zero amplitudes 1/√3 (from |0₁0₂⟩ and |1₁0₂⟩)  
– when qubit 2 is |1⟩ we have a single amplitude 1/√3 (from |0₁1₂⟩).

Thus

ρ₂ =Tr₁[|ψ⟩⟨ψ|]
    =⎡⎣P(0) ⟨0|ρ₂|1⟩
      ⟨1|ρ₂|0⟩ P(1)⎤⎦

with
 P(0)=|1/√3|²+|1/√3|²=2/3,  
 P(1)=|1/√3|²=1/3,

and the off-diagonal
 ⟨0|ρ₂|1⟩=⟨1|ρ₂|0⟩* =
   (1/√3)(1/√3)+(1/√3)⋅0 =1/3.

Hence in the {|0⟩,|1⟩} basis

ρ₂ =  ⎛ 2/3 1/3 ⎞  
       ⎝ 1/3 1/3 ⎠.

instruction: Proof that Q(sqrt(-11)) is a principal ideal domain
output:
Here is a short proof that the full ring of integers of K=ℚ(√−11) is a PID, by showing its class‐group is trivial via Minkowski’s bound.

1) Ring of integers and discriminant.  
Since −11≡1 mod 4, the ring of integers is  
  O_K = ℤ[ω], ω = (1+√−11)/2.  
Its (fundamental) discriminant is Δ = −11.

2) Minkowski’s bound for imaginary quadratic fields.  
In general, for an imaginary quadratic field of discriminant Δ<0, Minkowski’s theorem gives that every ideal‐class contains an integral ideal of norm ≤  
  M = (2/π)·√|Δ|.  
Here |Δ|=11, so  
  M = (2/π)·√11 ≃ (2/3.1416)·3.317 ≃ 2.11.  
Hence every ideal class of O_K has a representative integral ideal whose (absolute) norm N≤2.

3) No nontrivial ideals of norm 1 or 2.  
— Norm 1: the only ideal of norm 1 is the unit ideal (O_K itself).  
— Norm 2: a prime ideal 𝔭 dividing 2 would satisfy N(𝔭) = 2, and then (2)=𝔭² or 𝔭·𝔭′.  To see what happens, factor the minimal polynomial of ω over 𝔽₂:  
 ω satisfies x²+x+3=0 over ℤ, so mod 2 it is x² + x +1.  But x²+x+1 has no root in 𝔽₂, hence is irreducible.  Therefore 2 remains inert in O_K, and (2) itself is a prime ideal of norm N((2)) = 2² =4.  In particular there is no ideal of norm 2.

4) Conclusion on the class group.  
Minkowski says every class has a representative of norm ≤2, but the only possible norms in that range are 1 or 2—and we have seen the only norm‐1 ideal is principal, and there is no norm‐2 ideal at all.  Hence there are no nontrivial ideal classes, i.e. the class group is trivial.

5) Trivial class group ⇒ PID.  
A Dedekind domain whose ideal class group is trivial is exactly a principal ideal domain.  Thus O_K is a PID.

∎

instruction:
Alice and Bob have two dice. 

They roll the dice together, note the sum of the two values shown, and repeat.

For Alice to win, two consecutive turns (meaning, two consecutive sums) need to result in 7. For Bob to win, he needs to see an eight followed by a seven. Who do we expect to win this game?

You are required to provide an analysis which coincides with simulation results. You can supply multiple answers in successive iterations. You are allowed to run a simulation after 2 iterations. After each analysis, provide a reflection on the accuracy and completeness so we might improve in another iteration.  If so, end a reply with "CONTINUE TO ITERATION [x]" and wait for my input. When there is no more accuracy or completeness issue left to resolve and the mathematical analysis agrees with the simulation results, please end by typing "SOLVED". Always end with either "CONTINUE TO ITERATION [x]" or "SOLVED".
output:
Here’s a first‐pass Markov‐chain analysis:

Define states by what “partial pattern” has just been seen:

  S   = no relevant partial match yet  
  A1  = last roll was a 7 (Alice is one‐step from her win)  
  B1  = last roll was an 8 (Bob is one‐step from his win)

Let p7 = 6/36 = 1/6, p8 = 5/36, po = 25/36.

Let P_S, P_A1, P_B1 be the probability that Alice eventually wins starting from each state.

1) From S:  
   P_S = p7·P_A1 + p8·P_B1 + po·P_S  
   ⇒  P_S = (1/6)P_A1 + (5/36)P_B1 + (25/36)P_S  

2) From A1:  
  – If next is 7 (p7), Alice wins (prob=1)  
  – If next is 8 (p8), move to B1  
  – Otherwise (po), back to S  
  ⇒ P_A1 = (1/6)·1 + (5/36)·P_B1 + (25/36)·P_S

3) From B1:  
  – If next is 7 (p7), Bob wins ⇒ Alice’s prob=0  
  – If next is 8 (p8), stay in B1  
  – Otherwise (po), back to S  
  ⇒ P_B1 = (5/36)·P_B1 + (25/36)·P_S

Solve 3) first:  
 (1 − 5/36)P_B1 = (25/36)P_S  
 ⇒ (31/36)P_B1 = (25/36)P_S  
 ⇒ P_B1 = (25/31)·P_S

Plug into 1):  
  P_S = (1/6)P_A1 + (5/36)·[(25/31)P_S] + (25/36)P_S  
  ⇒ 11·P_S = 6·P_A1 + (125/31)P_S  
  ⇒ (216/31)P_S = 6·P_A1  
  ⇒ P_A1 = (36/31)·P_S

Now plug P_B1 and P_A1 into 2):  
  P_A1 = 1/6 + (5/36)·[(25/31)P_S] + (25/36)P_S  
       = 1/6 + (125/1116 + 775/1116) P_S  
       = 1/6 + (900/1116)P_S  
       = 1/6 + (25/31)P_S

Set equal to (36/31)P_S:  
 (36/31)P_S = 1/6 + (25/31)P_S  
 ⇒ (11/31)P_S = 1/6  
 ⇒ P_S = 31/66 ≈ 0.4697

Thus Alice’s win‐probability ≈0.4697, Bob’s ≈0.5303.  So Bob is favored.

Reflection on accuracy and completeness:  
 – The chain-of-states derivation is standard and algebra is straightforward.  
 – We should verify this against a Monte Carlo simulation to be sure no algebraic slip occurred.  
 – We might also consider edge cases (overlaps like 7–7–7…), but the Markov formulation handles overlaps correctly.  

CONTINUE TO ITERATION 2

instruction: A table-tennis championship for $2^n$ players is organized as a knock-out tournament with $n$ rounds, the last round being the final. Two players are chosen at random. Calculate the probability that they meet: (a) in the first round, (b) in the final, (c) in any round.
output:
Label the players A and B.  We assume all 2^n players are equally‐matched, so in any match each player wins with probability 1/2, and the initial bracket is a uniform random pairing.

1) Probability they actually play each other in round r  
   – First, the chance that in the _draw_ they are placed so as to _meet_ in round r (i.e. lie in the same block of size 2^r but in different halves of it) is  
     P_sch(r) = 2^{r−1}/(2^n−1).  
   – Then to _reach_ that match they each must win r–1 preceding rounds, which costs a factor (1/2)^{2(r−1)}.  
   Hence  
     P(meet in round r) = P_sch(r)·(1/2)^{2(r−1)}  
                      = 2^{r−1}/(2^n−1) · 1/2^{2r−2}  
                      = 1/[2^{r−1}(2^n−1)].

2) (a)  Round 1 (r=1):  
     P₁ = 1/(2^n−1).

   (b)  The final is r=n:  
     P_final = 1/[2^{n−1}(2^n−1)].

3)  The probability they meet _in some_ round is the sum over r=1…n:  
     ∑_{r=1}^n 1/[2^{r−1}(2^n−1)]  
     = (1 + 1/2 + 1/4 +···+1/2^{n−1})/(2^n−1)  
     = (2−2^{1−n})/(2^n−1)  
     = 1/2^{n−1}.  

Summary:  
(a) 1/(2^n−1)  
(b) 1/[2^{n−1}(2^n−1)]  
(c) 1/2^{n−1}

instruction: How can I generate a seaborn barplot that includes the values of the bar heights and confidence intervals?
output:
Here is a recipe in two steps:

 1.  Let seaborn compute and draw the bars + error‐bars for you (using its built-in bootstrapped 95% CI).  
 2.  “Harvest” the heights (and/or the CI endpoints) from the artists that seaborn drew and annotate them with `ax.text`.

---

## 1) A quick way to just annotate the bar‐heights

```python
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# example data
tips = sns.load_dataset("tips")

# draw barplot with 95% CI by default
ax = sns.barplot(x="day", y="total_bill", data=tips, capsize=.1)

# annotate each bar with its height
for p in ax.patches:
    h = p.get_height()
    ax.text(
        p.get_x() + p.get_width()/2.,  # x = center of bar
        h + 0.5,                        # y = just above the bar
        f"{h:.1f}",                     # the text
        ha="center"
    )

plt.ylim(0, None)
plt.show()
```

That will give you bars with the mean bill per day, 95% bootstrapped CI error bars, and the mean printed above each bar.

---

## 2) If you also want to *print the actual CI bounds* (e.g. [low, high] or “±”)

Seaborn does not expose the numeric CI’s it used. You have two choices:

a) Recompute your own group‐wise mean & CI, plot with Matplotlib’s `bar(..., yerr=…)` or seaborn’s `barplot(..., yerr=…)`, and then annotate;  
b) Hack into the Line2D objects that seaborn drew for the error bars.  

### 2a) Recompute the CI yourself

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats

# sample data
tips = sns.load_dataset("tips")

# 1) compute group stats
grp = (
    tips
    .groupby("day")["total_bill"]
    .agg(["mean","count","std"])
    .reset_index()
)
grp["se"] = grp["std"] / np.sqrt(grp["count"])
# for a 95% CI use the t‐distribution
ci_mult = stats.t.ppf(0.975, grp["count"] - 1)
grp["ci"] = grp["se"] * ci_mult

# 2) plot with yerr=CI
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(grp["day"], grp["mean"], yerr=grp["ci"], capsize=5)

# 3) annotate with mean ± CI
for idx, row in grp.iterrows():
    text = f"{row['mean']:.1f} ± {row['ci']:.1f}"
    ax.text(
        idx,                             # x‐position = integer index of bar
        row["mean"] + row["ci"] + 0.5,  # y‐position just above the upper error bar
        text,
        ha="center"
    )

ax.set_ylabel("total_bill")
plt.ylim(0, None)
plt.show()
```

This will give you exactly the mean and the half‐width of the 95% CI that you printed above each bar.

---

### 2b) (Advanced) Extract the CI from seaborn’s artists

Seaborn draws each error bar as a small Line2D with three segments (the vertical line + two caps).  In principle you can walk through `ax.lines`, find the lines and read off their y‐data.  Personally I find (2a) above much clearer, but here is a sketch:

```python
ax = sns.barplot(x="day", y="total_bill", data=tips, capsize=.1)

# loop over the "lines" that seaborn drew for CIs
# every error bar is 3 lines: [cap1, stem, cap2]
lines = ax.lines
for i in range(0, len(lines), 3):
    cap1, stem, cap2 = lines[i], lines[i+1], lines[i+2]
    # the vertical stem has two y‐values: [lower, upper]
    y_lower, y_upper = stem.get_ydata()
    # the x coordinate of that stem segment
    x = stem.get_xdata().mean()
    # annotate above the top cap
    ax.text(
        x,
        y_upper + 0.5,
        f"[{y_lower:.1f}, {y_upper:.1f}]",
        ha="center",
        color="gray"
    )

# now also annotate the bar‐heights if you like
for p in ax.patches:
    h = p.get_height()
    ax.text(
        p.get_x() + p.get_width()/2.,
        h + 0.3,
        f"{h:.1f}",
        ha="center",
        color="black"
    )

plt.ylim(0, None)
plt.show()
```

---

instruction: Can you give me some Seaborn code for plotting the ECDF of a KDE-augmented dataset?
output:
Here’s a minimal example showing how you can “augment” a 1-D data array by sampling from its KDE, and then plot the ECDF of the augmented dataset with Seaborn. In this snippet I also overlay the ECDF of the original data for comparison.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde

# 1) Create some toy data
rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
data = rng.normal(loc=0, scale=1, size=200)

# 2) Fit a KDE to your data
kde = gaussian_kde(data)

# 3) Draw new samples from the KDE
n_aug = 1000
aug_samples = kde.resample(n_aug).ravel()   # shape (n_aug,)

# 4) Concatenate original + augmented
augmented = np.concatenate([data, aug_samples])

# 5) Plot the ECDFs
plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))

# original ECDF (dashed)
sns.ecdfplot(data=data,
             stat="proportion",
             complementary=False,
             linestyle="--",
             label="original")

# augmented ECDF (solid)
sns.ecdfplot(data=augmented,
             stat="proportion",
             complementary=False,
             label=f"augmented (+{n_aug})")

plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("ECDF")
plt.legend()
plt.title("ECDF: original vs. KDE-augmented")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Explanation of the key steps:

1.  We fit a `scipy.stats.gaussian_kde` to the raw data.
2.  We then draw `n_aug` new points from that KDE.
3.  We concatenate the original and the drawn samples.
4.  Finally we call Seaborn’s `ecdfplot` on both the original and augmented arrays.

You can of course tweak:

-  The KDE bandwidth by passing `bw_method=` into `gaussian_kde`.
-  The line styles, colors, etc., to suit your taste.
-  Or even only plot the augmented ECDF if that’s all you need.

instruction: Write a function to generate cryptographically secure random numbers.
output:
Here’s a simple Python example using the built-in secrets module (available in 3.6+) to get cryptographically secure random integers, bytes or hex-strings:

```python
import secrets

def secure_randint(min_inclusive: int, max_inclusive: int) -> int:
    """
    Return a cryptographically secure random integer N such that
    min_inclusive <= N <= max_inclusive.
    """
    if min_inclusive > max_inclusive:
        raise ValueError("min_inclusive must be <= max_inclusive")
    # secrets.randbelow(n) returns a value in [0, n)
    range_size = max_inclusive - min_inclusive + 1
    return min_inclusive + secrets.randbelow(range_size)

def secure_random_bytes(n_bytes: int) -> bytes:
    """
    Return n_bytes of cryptographically secure random data.
    """
    return secrets.token_bytes(n_bytes)

def secure_random_hex(n_bytes: int) -> str:
    """
    Return a hex‐encoded string of length 2*n_bytes, cryptographically secure.
    """
    return secrets.token_hex(n_bytes)


# Example usage:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Random int between 1 and 100:", secure_randint(1, 100))
    print("16 random bytes      :", secure_random_bytes(16))
    print("16-byte hex string  :", secure_random_hex(16))
```

Explanation:

- secrets.randbelow(n) returns an integer in [0, n) using the OS’s CSPRNG.  
- token_bytes(n) returns n raw bytes.  
- token_hex(n) is just token_bytes(n) hex-encoded for you.  

Under the hood secrets uses os.urandom() (or the Windows CryptoAPI) so the values are suitable for cryptographic use.

instruction: How to set seeds for random generator in Python in threads?
output:
In CPython the default `random` module keeps one global, shared RNG state.  If you just call `random.seed(…)` inside each thread you are mutating that one global state and you still have races.  What you almost always want instead is one independent RNG per thread.  There are two common idioms:

1.  Pass each thread its own `random.Random` instance.  
2.  Store a per‐thread RNG in thread‐local storage.

---

1) Passing an RNG into your thread function  
```python
import threading
import random

def worker(rng, num_samples=5):
    # use rng instead of random
    samples = [rng.random() for _ in range(num_samples)]
    print(f"Thread {threading.current_thread().name} ->", samples)

threads = []
for i in range(4):
    # seed each thread’s RNG differently (e.g. based on i)
    rng = random.Random(1234 + i)
    t = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(rng,), name=f"T{i}")
    t.start()
    threads.append(t)

for t in threads:
    t.join()
```
Here each thread is using its own `rng.random()` calls, seeded to a distinct value.

---

2) Using `threading.local` to hide the RNG in thread‐local storage  
```python
import threading
import random

_local = threading.local()

def get_thread_rng(seed=None):
    """Return a Random instance unique to this thread."""
    if not hasattr(_local, "rng"):
        _local.rng = random.Random(seed if seed is not None else threading.get_ident())
    return _local.rng

def worker(num_samples=5):
    # you can pass a seed in if you want full control
    rng = get_thread_rng()
    samples = [rng.random() for _ in range(num_samples)]
    print(f"{threading.current_thread().name}:", samples)

threads = []
for i in range(4):
    # Optionally you can pass seed=i or any scheme to get repeatability
    t = threading.Thread(target=worker, name=f"T{i}")
    t.start()
    threads.append(t)

for t in threads:
    t.join()
```
Each call to `get_thread_rng()` in a given thread returns the same `Random` object but threads don’t share state.

---

NumPy’s new Generator API (>=1.17) works the same way:

```python
import threading
import numpy as np

_local = threading.local()

def get_nprng(seed=None):
    if not hasattr(_local, "rng"):
        # PCG64 is the default bit‐generator
        _local.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed if seed is not None else threading.get_ident())
    return _local.rng

def worker():
    rng = get_nprng()
    print(f"{threading.current_thread().name}:", rng.random(5))

threads = []
for i in range(4):
    t = threading.Thread(target=worker, name=f"N{i}")
    t.start()
    threads.append(t)

for t in threads:
    t.join()
```

---

Key takeaways:

- Don’t rely on `random.seed()` in each thread to isolate state.
- Create separate RNG instances (via `random.Random` or NumPy’s `default_rng`) and give each thread its own.
- You can manage these instances by passing them in or by using `threading.local()`.

instruction: Regex to delect all <g> elements containing a string `transform="matrix(0.998638,0,0,-0.998638,0.39215,439.799858)"` please. there can be line breaks too.
output:
Here’s a single‐regex (PCRE/JavaScript/Python) solution that will strip out any `<g>…</g>` block whose opening tag contains exactly

  transform="matrix(0.998638,0,0,-0.998638,0.39215,439.799858)"

—even if there are line breaks anywhere inside the tag or the contents:

Regex (with “dot matches newline” enabled):

    (?is)<g\b(?=[^>]*\btransform="matrix\(0\.998638,0,0,-0\.998638,0\.39215,439\.799858\)").*?</g>

Explanation of the pieces:

  • (?is)                – i = case-insensitive (probably not needed, but harmless)  
                         – s = “dot matches newline”  
  • <g\b                 – matches “<g” with a word boundary (so you don’t catch `<glyph>`)  
  • (?=[^>]*\btransform="matrix\(...\)")  
                         – a lookahead requiring that before the first “>” you have that exact transform=…  
  • .*?                   – now consume up to the matching `</g>` (non-greedy)  
  • </g>                  – closing tag  

Usage examples:

1) Perl/PCRE

    $new_svg = $old_svg;
    $new_svg =~ s{(?is)<g\b(?=[^>]*\btransform="matrix\(0\.998638,0,0,-0\.998638,0\.39215,439\.799858\)").*?</g>}{}g;

2) JavaScript (modern engines supporting the “s” flag)

    svgString = svgString.replace(
      /<g\b(?=[^>]*\btransform="matrix\(0\.998638,0,0,-0\.998638,0\.39215,439\.799858\)").*?<\/g>/gis,
      ''
    );

3) Python

    import re
    pattern = re.compile(
      r'<g\b(?=[^>]*\btransform="matrix\(0\.998638,0,0,-0\.998638,0\.39215,439\.799858\)").*?</g>',
      re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL
    )
    new_svg = pattern.sub('', old_svg)

Adjust escaping or flags as needed for your environment.

instruction: write pcre regex for not containing  C:\
output:
Here’s a straight‐forward PCRE solution using a negative look‐ahead.  This will match any string that does *not* contain the substring `C:\`:

```
/^(?!.*C:\\).*$/
```

Explanation:  
 1. `^`            – start of string  
 2. `(?!.*C:\\)`  – fail if anywhere ahead there is `C:\`  
 3. `.*`          – match the rest of the string (any characters)  
 4. `$`           – end of string  

Note:  
• In many programming languages (e.g. PHP, Java, JavaScript), you’ll need to escape the backslash twice in a string literal. For example in PHP:

   $re = "/^(?!.*C:\\\\).*$/";
  
• If you need to allow an empty string as a “non-containing” match, use `.*`. If you require at least one character, use `.+` instead:

   `/^(?!.*C:\\).+$/`

Considering Tools For Thought and the organization of personal knowledge, please list some best practice frameworks that detail a system of procedures and best practice.  Please make a comprehensive list of frameworks and summarize the top three in more detail.
output:
Below is a non-exhaustive list of popular “Tools-for-Thought” or Personal Knowledge Management (PKM) frameworks—each defines a repeatable system of procedures and best practices for capturing, organizing, distilling and retrieving ideas:

1. Zettelkasten Method (Luhmann/Ahrens)  
2. PARA (Projects, Areas, Resources, Archives) by Tiago Forte  
3. CODE (Capture, Organize, Distill, Express) – the backbone of Building a Second Brain  
4. Building a Second Brain (BASB) – Forte’s umbrella methodology (PARA + Progressive Summarization, etc.)  
5. Linking Your Thinking (LYT) by Nick Milo  
6. Progressive Summarization (PS) by Tiago Forte  
7. GTD (Getting Things Done) by David Allen applied to knowledge work  
8. Commonplace Book (traditional “book of quotations/notable ideas”)  
9. Atomic Notes (Conor White-Sullivan)  
10. Smart Notes (Sönke Ahrens’s interpretation of Zettelkasten)  
11. Cornell Note-Taking System (cue‐note‐summary triad)  
12. Mind-Mapping (Tony Buzan)  
13. C4 (Capture, Curate, Create, Communicate) by Amber McCue  
14. PKM Diamond (Capture ↔ Reflect ↔ Link ↔ Share cycle)  
15. AIRE (Acquire, Interact, Reuse, Evolve)  
16. Map of Contents (MOC) by Roam/Obsidian community  
17. LATCH (Location, Alphabet, Time, Category, Hierarchy indexing)  
18. Feynman Technique (explain to learn)  
19. PARA-lite variants (RAPID, ARC, etc.)  

—  
Below are deeper dives into the three most widely adopted, battle-tested frameworks:

1. Zettelkasten Method  
   • Origin: Developed by sociologist Niklas Luhmann and popularized by Sönke Ahrens (“How to Take Smart Notes”).  
   • Core idea: Build a web of atomic, permanently-valuable notes (zettels), each capturing one concept or idea, given its own ID.  
   • Workflow:  
     1. Fleeting notes – capture raw inputs fast.  
     2. Literature notes – summarize sources in your own words.  
     3. Permanent notes – distill ideas into standalone, cross-linked slips.  
   • Linking: Each note links to related notes bi-directionally; over time a densely connected “second brain” emerges.  
   • Benefits: Encourages depth of thought, serendipitous connections, prevents “topic islands.”  
   • Tools: Physical card box; digital tools like Obsidian, Zettlr, The Archive.  

2. PARA Method (Projects, Areas, Resources, Archives)  
   • Creator: Tiago Forte. Simple folder-and-tag schema to organize ALL your digital files & notes.  
   • Four top-level categories:  
     – Projects: Short-term commitments with clear outcomes (e.g. “Write annual report”)  
     – Areas: Long-term spheres of activity & responsibility (e.g. “Health,” “Finance,” “Team management”)  
     – Resources: Topic-oriented reference material you might someday use (e.g. “Marketing research,” “Python snippets”)  
     – Archives: Inactive items from the other three categories.  
   • Key practices:  
     – Review Projects/Areas weekly.  
     – Move items promptly into Archives when done.  
     – Use consistent naming conventions and links (e.g. “YYYY-MM-DD – Meeting Notes”).  
   • Benefits: Universal (works in any note-taking app or file system), keeps “active” work front-and-center, minimal cognitive overhead.  

3. Linking Your Thinking (LYT)  
   • Creator: Nick Milo. A modular, app-agnostic PKM workflow built around “Maps of Content” (MOCs) and layered note-types.  
   • Components:  
     – Fleeting Notes: Quick captures (same as Zettelkasten).  
     – Evergreen Notes: Polished, semi-permanent insights (similar to permanent Zettel).  
     – **Maps of Content (MOCs):** Topical index pages that organize links to related notes in a hierarchical or “table of contents” style.  
     – **Linking:** Heavy emphasis on in-note links and back-links.  
   • Workflow phases:  
     1. Capture → Fleeting Notes  
     2. Organize → Sort into MOCs or draft evergreen notes  
     3. Distill → Refine evergreen notes, update MOCs  
     4. Synthesize → Combine multiple notes for writing or projects  
   • Benefits: Highly visual “dashboard” via MOCs, clear separation of note-types, encourages both structure (MOCs) and serendipity (linking).  

—  
Each of these frameworks has proven records of helping knowledge workers turn a flood of information into a reusable, generative “second brain.” You can mix and match—e.g. use PARA to structure your vault, Zettelkasten to take permanent notes, and LYT’s MOCs as high-level dashboards.

instruction: Introduce Ethan, including his experience-level with software development methodologies like waterfall and agile development. Describe the major differences between traditional waterfall and agile software developments. In his opinion, what are the most notable advantages and disadvantages of each methodology?
output:
Here’s a profile of Ethan and his take on waterfall vs. agile software development:

1. Introduction to Ethan  
   • Title & Experience  
     – Senior Software Engineer with 10 years in the industry  
     – Has worked in finance, healthcare, and e-commerce domains  
   • Methodology Background  
     – Early career spent on traditional waterfall projects (regulated environments, fixed-price contracts)  
     – Past 6 years leading Scrum and Kanban teams in fast-moving startups  
     – Certified Scrum Master (CSM) and Lean practitioner  

2. Major Differences Between Waterfall and Agile  
   1. Project Structure  
      • Waterfall: Sequential phases (Requirements → Design → Implementation → Testing → Deployment → Maintenance)  
      • Agile: Iterative cycles/sprints (plan → develop → test → review → adapt)  
   2. Requirements & Scope  
      • Waterfall: All requirements defined up-front; scope locked after approval  
      • Agile: Requirements evolve; backlog reprioritized each sprint  
   3. Documentation vs. Working Software  
      • Waterfall: Heavy emphasis on comprehensive documentation at each phase  
      • Agile: “Working software over comprehensive documentation”; minimal but essential docs  
   4. Customer Involvement  
      • Waterfall: Stakeholder reviews at phase-gates (typically infrequent)  
      • Agile: Continuous collaboration with product owner/end users every sprint  
   5. Testing Approach  
      • Waterfall: Testing occurs after build phase (often late in schedule)  
      • Agile: Continuous testing and integration throughout development  
   6. Change Management  
      • Waterfall: Change control boards; formal change requests; costly to pivot  
      • Agile: Embraces change, rapid reprioritization, “fail fast” learning  

3. Ethan’s View: Advantages & Disadvantages  
   A. Waterfall  
      Advantages  
        • Predictability: Clear timelines, budgets, and deliverables  
        • Easy to manage: Milestones and gate reviews suit fixed-price or heavily regulated projects  
        • Thorough documentation: Good for long-lifecycle maintenance teams  
      Disadvantages  
        • Inflexible: Late-stage changes are expensive and disruptive  
        • Risk of requirement mismatch: Stakeholders may misunderstand initial specs  
        • Late testing: Bugs and design flaws often surface near deployment, risking schedule slips  

   B. Agile  
      Advantages  
        • Adaptability: Can respond quickly to market or user-driven changes  
        • Early value delivery: Working increments get in users’ hands sooner  
        • Continuous feedback: Frequent demos uncover issues before they snowball  
        • Team empowerment: Self-organizing teams often increase morale and ownership  
      Disadvantages  
        • Less predictability: Harder to forecast exact scope, cost, and delivery date up-front  
        • Potential for scope creep: Ongoing backlog changes require strict product-owner discipline  
        • Scaling challenges: Coordinating dozens of teams requires additional frameworks (e.g., SAFe, LeSS)  
        • Documentation trade-offs: Regulatory or hand-off scenarios may suffer from lighter docs  

Overall, Ethan believes that waterfall still has a place in large, compliance-driven projects, but for most web and mobile initiatives today, agile’s responsiveness and user-centric approach deliver higher business value and lower risk over the long run.

“Your APP_BUILD_SCRIPT is pointing to a file that ndk-build cannot find.”

In your particular case Gradle is telling ndk-build:

  APP_BUILD_SCRIPT=E:\Dhruvin kheni\…\app\src\main\jni\Android.mk

and then ndk-build says “I looked in there and there is no Android.mk.”

You have three choices to fix this:

  1.  Actually put an Android.mk at that exact path

        app/src/main/jni/Android.mk

     — or —

  2.  If your JNI folder lives somewhere else, change your build.gradle so that
     it points at the real location:

     ```groovy
     android {
       …
       externalNativeBuild {
         ndkBuild {
           // make sure this matches exactly where YOUR Android.mk really lives
           path "src/main/cpp/Android.mk"
         }
       }
     }
     ```

     If you leave off `file(…)` Gradle will treat that as a module‐relative path.

  3.  If you are not actually using ndk-build and instead want CMake, remove the
     `externalNativeBuild.ndkBuild { … }` block entirely, drop in a
     `CMakeLists.txt` and switch to

     ```groovy
     externalNativeBuild {
       cmake {
         path "src/main/cpp/CMakeLists.txt"
       }
     }
     ```

A few gotchas on Windows:

  •  Paths with spaces can sometimes break ndk-build’s quoting, so you may
     find it easier to move the project to a path without spaces.  
  •  Always use forward slashes (`/`) in your Gradle script; Gradle will
     translate them for Windows.  
  •  Verify with File Explorer (or a console `dir`) that the .mk file is
     really where you think it is.

Once your `APP_BUILD_SCRIPT` truly points at an existing Android.mk, the “unknown file” error will go away and ndk-build will proceed.
